THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with
Juan Tizol
by Patricia Willard
Reel 1-3
November 15, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
This is the Oral History with Juan Tizol, and this is November 14th, 1978.
Juan, the birth date that I found in two encyclopedias ...
You have to talk louder.
Okay. You were born January 22, 1900? Is that right?
That's right.
Okay, and in San Juan, Puerto Rico?
San Juan, Puerto Rico
Had your family been in Puerto Rico for a long time?
Oh yes. Most certainly, they had been there for a long time, but there are quite a few that are dead now, you know.
I see. Did you have brothers and sisters?
I had a sister, and she is dead, too.
So there were just two children in the family?
Yes, just two children.
And what was your sister's name?
Remedio.
R-e-m-e-d-i-o?
D-i-o. Yeah.
And how about your parents? What were their names?
My parents were Juan Tizol, and my mother was Manuela Martinez.
Oh. And were either of your parents musicians or did they play an instrument?

Oh, in my family, quite a few of them were musicians. They used to teach me some things when I was small. My uncle was the, what do you call it, about the best musician in the country there. He was the Director for the symphony, Director for the Municipal band, and he would do it without an arrangement, you know -- I don't mean for the popular things, though; he arranged most of the legit stuff.
That was your Uncle Manuel?
Manuel Tizol, yeah.
And that was, what? The symphony orchestra of Puerto Rico?
Yeah, uh huh.
And where did he study music? Did he study in a school in Puerto Rico?
Oh, he studied there in Puerto Rico.
Do you know what school he studied at?
No, he studied by with a professional man,
I forgot where he is now, but he studied in Puerto Rico, but I know the musician.
Uh huh. And so your uncle was the leader of the Municipal Band and the symphony orchestra?
Yeah.
What other relatives of yours were in music? Did your parents play instruments, too?

My parents -- he wasn't a musician. He was an accountant, or something like that. But Manuel, he plays the cello, he plays my trombone, oh, he plays quite a few things --he played a bassoon. But most of the stuff he was just directing, you know? And he used to furnish the musicians at the theatre, when the opera was coming in, he furnished the musicians, like he was the contractor for anything that came to the theatre, he would bring the musicians in and put them in.
And he taught you what you know. Did he give you lessons?
Oh, yeah -- sure.
How old were you when you first started to play and study?

Oh, I guess I was about 18 years old. He taught me how to do solfege (unintelligible), you know? And then I learned my instrument in school. They gave me a trombone, and I knew, by being around my uncle with the Municipal Band, I
always asked him about the scale on the trombone, how you did it and so forth; and I used to practice myself.
So they put me in the school and they gave me a trombone, and I did so well in the school that my uncle brought me in to the Municipal Band, you know?
How old were you when you went to the Municipal Band?

Oh, I was about 18 or 20 years old. He brought me into the Municipal Band, and I played, and I was like a second trombone, or second euphonium, 'cause I used to play a euphonium. You know what euphonium a euphonian is? It's like a baritone.
Uh huh. You played the euphonium before you played the trombone?
No, I played the trombone in the school.
Oh, I see -- and then you played the euphonium in the band.
I played the euphonium in the Municipal Band. And once in awhile, when the opera come, my uncle would put to let me play (UNINTELLIGIBLE) third trombone, you know.
Oh, for the opera. When the opera came, was that an opera company from Puerto Rico or from the States?
No, from New York. The regular opera company, like with Anna Pavlova and things like that -- oh, they came from New York. The best, and the best directors, and so forth.
So you played also for the ballet?
Yeah, for the ballet.
When Did Pavlova danced?
Pardon?
When Pavlova danced, you played?

Well, yeah; a little bit. But I mean, I was way down there -- the trombone; I was not a first trombone then, you know? I was learning. But my uncle just put me in there because he thought I could make it.
That's marvelous. Did -- you didn't pick trombone, though, yourself? They just gave you a trombone and said to play.
They gave me a trombone at school.
So that was when you were younger than 18?
Yeah.
How old were you when they gave you the trombone?

Well, that I cannot say. Also, I played violin in the orchestra in school. Yeah, I was learning violin, but it was a little too hard, and I dropped it, you know? Because with the trombone, then I started playing in the orchestra for the dancers and so forth, and I was making a little bit of money, so I said there was no reason for me to fool with this violin, so I stopped playing and started playing trombone in bands and with small orchestras and so forth,
and I was doing very well, so I dropped the violin. Only the violin I was just playing in school; I was playing first violin, but no, I couldn't do so good on it.
I think Rose remembers something here. What was it?
You forgot to tell her, Juan, that your uncle taught you all you know.
Oh, exactly. He taught me everything.
At what point did you decide you wanted to be a musician professionally?
When, did you say?
When did you decide that that was what you wanted to be?
[When I called a] conference in the family -- my uncle, my cousin, and quite a few relatives -- the family Tizol, they were musicians, too, so it seems to me that I inherited it, you know?
I see. What other members of the family were musicians?
Musicians? Frank Tizol -- he was a bass player and a trombone player, too; a very good bass player.
An arranger.
Arranger, and everything.
Who was Frank? Was he an uncle or a cousin?
He was a cousin. Helived in New York;
after he came to New York, he died right in there.
Was he Manuel's son, or was he ...
No, no. His father was the father of Frank, he was the best criminal lawyer in the country.
Oh? What was his name?

José de Jesus Tizol. Then he became a Senator, and when he used to talk about politics and so forth in Washington, they bring him from Puerto Rico, and he was the lawyer for the Commission from Puerto Rico.

So your Uncle Manuel got you in to the Municipal Orchestra and the musical band and the symphony orchestra, and you played for the ballet and the opera, and you were studying with him, all of this time, right?
Right.
And he taught you, besides your own instruments, he taught you arranging?
No, no, I never did arranging. No.
Never did, huh? When did you start writing music?
Oh, I started writing music when I started with Duke Ellington.
That was the very first time you wrote?
Well, I wrote a dance, I wrote one of these Puerto Rico dances; I wrote it when I was in the

Municipal Band, and I was dedicated to an old school girl that I used to like. Her name was Julia -- called her Julietta, "Julita," and my uncle and I named the tune Julietta On my own, but I arranged it I could not arrange : for the band, because I could write the melody and the song and so forth, but not for arranging. He had arranged it for a 45 piece band to play, because the band used to play on Wednesdays and Sundays at the Plaza, and that particular night they played my danzon, called Julietta. "Julita."
Oh, that's wonderful. How old were you when you wrote Julietta? "Julita" ?
When I wrote the tune?
Uh huh.
Well, I was, I guess 20 years old.
And you were named after Saint Juan? Right? San Juan?
What?
The reason your name is Juan.
I was named just like my father -- my father was named Juan.
I see, because I read someplace that you were named after the saint, but then, your father probably was, too, right?
Yeah.
Huh?
Say 'yeah'. You were named after Saint John -- San Juan.
Oh, San Juan.
Yeah. Yeah.
And so was your father?
Yeah.
I know that you came, according to what I read in books, you came to this country with the Marie Lucas orchestra, is that right?

No, no. We didn't come with Marie Lucas; we came together to the Howard Theatre in Washington, D.C. -- 13 Puerto Rican musicians, you know? At the Howard Theatre, and we used to play in the pit, and they used to have an orchestra, a jazz orchestra in one of the boxes. They played jazz tunes, and we'd play an overture or a little symphony, or a little something legit.
Oh. So what year was it that you came to the United States with the Puerto Rican band?
Oh, that was in 1920. I guess so, something like that.
So it was shortly after you went into the Muncipal Band, and then you came to the United States?
Yeah, yeah.
Did you stay here then, or did you go back to Puerto Rico?
No. From then on, I stayed. I stayed in Washington, then from there, from the Howard Theatre they didn't use then with the Puerto Rican musicians and then I stayed there

and my name got acquainted with the small jazz bands, and so forth; the orchestra dance, bands, and so they started giving me little jobs because, after all, I was using valve to the trombone, and they figured the valve trombone wouldn't be no good for jazz. But the thing. they used to give me violin parts, and I could play all of them things.
And I could do on a valve trombone what a slide trombone couldn't do, you know? So they started putting me in bands and so forth.
Did you choose valve trombone rather than slide trombone, or did that just happen to be the kind of trombone they gave you?
See, in my country, they used to use most of the time valve instruments, like the baritone, the trombone and things like that. The slide trombone -- all they used that for was in the army bands.
Oh, I see.
But in the Municipal Band, all I learned was the 3-valve trombone.
How did you and the other musicians happen to come from Puerto Rico to the Howard Theatre?

One of the musicians that was working for a long time at the Howard Theatre before we came there -- the owner of the theatre sent this fellow to Puerto Rico to get 13 musicians, and we got them from part of the Municipal Band, he got me and quite a few others -- some of the best
musicians in the Municipal Band, he got, and they brought us to the Howard Theatre, and the way we came to the Howard Theatre, by boat, but we were stowaways.
How did that happen?

Well, we got the fellow, who ran one of the [printer] on boats, he got the bags and things like that the night before -- got the bags and everything in the boat, and we came in the boat at 11:00 o'clock at night, and the ship didn't leave until the next day at five o'clock.

So we stayed in one room, you know? One cabin, we stayed there all that time until five o'clock that afternoon, when the boat left. Nobody knew, but I think everybody was getting paid on the boat, you know?
Uh huh.

So, from the cabin, after the boat was so many miles away, they took us where the farmers and the coal passers miners and the engineers were all sleeping downstairs in this big room, so we used that bed -- while the one man was working, I'd take his cabin and I'd sleep there. When he came in from his guard shift, then I would get up from there and go to another one, until we got to New York. And they'd bring us plenty of food. They treated us very nicely.
Just like I say, everybody was paid in there.
So that was the way the crew made a little extra money, I guess, right?
Yeah. The crew was making the money, you

know? But we didn't care, as long as we got to New York. When we got to New York, somebody asked you who had been to New York before, and when they asked, I said, "Me". And they said, "Oh, well you know how to get out of here, then", and I said, "Well, all you have to do is walk out on the pier." So, I walked off the pier and nothing happened. It was just like I say -- everybody was getting paid. The people in front of the pier that examine people -- "Where are you going," and so forth, like that -- they didn't say a thing; they just let me go through.

And we got together, and we went to -- we got on a train; some of the boys got on a train, but I wasn't supposed to get to Washington right away on that particular trip, so I stayed in New York and the rest of the fellows went to the Howard Theatre.

And so I stayed in New York working anywhere -- I worked in what do you call, the Sunshine Biscuit Company, or something like that -- the National Biscuit Company; I worked in all kinds of factories and stuff like that.
Why did you stay in New York and work in factories instead of going to Washington?
No, because they didn't need me right away at that particular time, you know?
Oh, I see.
They didn't need me then, and I

then I didn't have the instrument. I didn't have any instrument then, and so I had to make enough money, and my family sent some money, and I went to the fellows that make instruments, Carl Fischer, Cal Fisher, and they got me this trombone for $50 -- brand new! They got me this trombone, and then after that, I was working, and they said, "Juan, we want you to come to Washington to join the band".
So I went over there and instead of a case, I got a bag, you know, and I put my trombone in there and went to Washington.
Did you know anybody in New York when you got there?
Oh, when I got to New York, I was working in this cracker business, the National Biscuit Company and different places, and I made acquaintances.
But when you first got to New York, did you know anybody?

When I first got to New York, I had a cousin in there. I had a cousin there, and he met me at the pier when I first came in there, but I had lost the money gambling on the boat, and I said, "The only thing is I lost all my money, so I don't know where I'll be able to stay", and he said, "Well, we'll get you someplace", so he took me where he was living himself.
Was that your cousin, Frank?
No, cousin Tony.
Tony?
Tony. Antonio, he was.
Antonio Tizol?
Oh sure, yeah. He was the son of the band leader, my uncle, you know?
Oh, I see. Was Antonio also a musician?
No, no. He was -- what do you call them? An accountant, I think it is. Accountant, uh huh.
Oh, I see. So how long did you work at the National Biscuit Company?
Oh, just long enough for me to make enough money for me to buy a trombone, you know?
How long was that?
Oh, [not long] -- at that time, I wasn't making too much money.
What did you do at the National Biscuit Company?
For instance, you know the dough?
Uh huh.

You get in there and throw it in one place, and from there, you make the little crackers and so forth -- oh, different things they put you in, you know? So I got out of there, and of course, I wasn't making enough
money there. But I worked at a lot of things there to make a living, anyhow.
Do you remember the name of the ship that you came to New York on?
The Catalina, I think.
Catalina?
Yeah.
Was it a regular passenger ship?

Oh, yeah, a regular ship. They used to leave every Wednesday for New York, and other boats used to leave for New York. Oh, it's a lot of trouble at that particular time, and there were no airplanes then to travel in.
So what did you think of New York in 1920?

Oh, I thought New York was -- I left there the first time because I thought New York was going to drown me; it was just a little too much for me, and then, besides, not working regularly, you know? Because when I left -- it was a good thing my family packed my suitcase with a lot of cheese and guava jelly and all different things, and I ate that for a long time. We had nothing to eat, just ate that stuff, but I got by, after all.
Did you hear any music while you were in New York?
Did I what?
Did you listen to music in New
York? Did you go to hear music any place?
No, no. I was too interested in trying to get a hold of some money. So I don't know.
When you got your trombone, then, from Carl Fischer, it was right after that, then, that you went to Washington?

Yeah, I went to Washington. That's when I started really playing with different orchestras, and there was where I met Duke Ellington. Duke Ellington was playing this particular box, like I told you before, in a box with five musicians, and Duke Ellington was the piano player with a jazz band. And we would play a symphony or an overture or something like that.
There used to be a supper show in the afternoon, and that was where I met my wife -- in the theatre.
Oh? How did you and Rose meet?
Oh, she ...

A friend of ours introduced us. A friend of mine, rather, introduced us. She was going with one of the fellows in the band, and she said, 'I want you to meet another fellow in the band.' So that's the way I met Juan.
I see. The group that you were playing with -- the Puerto Rico music, they were still the Puerto Rican musicians?
Yeah.
Did they have a name for their group?
No, no. It was the Howard Theatre Orchestra.
Oh, I see.

There used to be a supper show at 6:30 in the afternoon; they'd play a picture, but we didn't have no music for the picture; we just played anything -- while the picture was going, we played a little symphony or something like that, and when some shows used to come in, like Marie Lucas, then she got the piano player with the orchestra.
Oh, with the orchestra that you were in?
Yeah.
I see.

That's with the symphony orchestra, I mean, the Howard Theatre Orchestra. She was the conductor and the piano player, and when shows used to come in, we'd play for the shows. Just like -- whats some of the shows? Name some. Well, anyhow ...
You mean the stage shows?
Yeah.
Do you remember any of the people, the stars of any of them?
No, I can't remember; can't remember.
" Shuffle Along, I remember, (unintelligible). Blake.
Oh, yeah -- Eubie Griffin.
Yeah, and Eubie Blake. Yeah.
And was he playing piano in that?
Yeah.
I see. And so was he playing on stage, or was he playing in the pit?
No, he played in the pit.
Eubie, too? Eubie Blake, too?
He was down in the pit.
Uh huh. So Duke's band -- so what other band beside Duke's band played in there while you were in that?
Well, at that particular time when I was with Duke, it was only about five pieces; and that's when I really got acquainted with Duke.
Who was the leader of the band that Duke was playing piano for?
Well, I imagine that he was the leader.
He was the leader?
Yeah.
I see. Sonny Greer was in that group, right?
Sonny Greer? I don't remember if Sonny Greer was. Sonny Greer was working in a different band then; we called them 'gigs', you know? Gigs with a different
orchestra.
But I thought Sonny Greer worked at the Howard, and Duke ...
Well, he was in there for quite a while, but that was after the Puerto Ricans got away, you know?
Oh.
That's right. he was playing there at the Howard Theatre.
So the first time you met Duke, though; Duke was the leader of a five piece group.
Yeah.
Do you remember who the other four musicians were?
No, but there was a very good drummer, who I can't remember, and a good trumpet player in New York, but I've forgotten what his name was. Do you remember, Rose? The trumpet player?
No, because I don't even remember Duke Ellington.
Did you used to go to the theatre a lot, Rose? To the Howard?
No, I would only go to a supper show. They had a supper show about from five to six, just an hour -- that was just the only time I went, see, because
I was going to school, and so forth and so on, you know, and then I had to go home. You know how it is. Just can't be staying out all that time.
I see. So you met Duke then. Do you remember what year that would have been? Well, you got to the Howard around 1920 or 1921?

I mean, I met Duke at that particular time when I was down at the Howard Theatre, and the way I got to join Duke, because we opened a business, between my wife and me, we opened a delicatessen store on Rhode Island Avenue.
Oh, that was a long time after that.

But that's all right. It'll come to me. We opened a store, and while we was there a while, I was there one day, the telephone rang and it was Duke Ellington asking me if I could come over and join the band, because at that particular time, he said he needed me in the band because he was ready to go with the Ziegfield Follies, and in that show, and another show called Showgirl with Ruby Keeler and that comedian -- oh, what's his name -- they called him Mr. Schnozzola, you know?
Oh, Jimmy Durante!

Jimmy Durante. Yes, he was the comedian in that particular show, and so, I decided, and I left Rose to take charge of the delicatessen and to try to sell it, and she stayed in Washington while I was with Duke
Ellington, until I got myself together, and she came over and met me there in New York.
Several books say that you were in the Marie Lucas Orchestra and that you toured with Marie Lucas. Is that true?
What?
Marie Lucas. Where was she from? Was she from Puerto Rico?
No, no. She is American.
Did she ever lead a band that you played in? Was she ever the leader of a band?
Yes, she was the leader, yeah.
I see. So did you leave the Howard and work with Marie Lucas?
I worked there with Marie Lucas while I was in the pit band.
But you didn't work anywhere else with her?

Yeah, that's right. I worked in Atlantic City and I worked there in New York; she came -- she brought a band in a nightclub in Washington, and I got in there, in that orchestra, and from there, I think we went to Atlantic City, and I worked with her in a nightclub in Atlantic City.
About how long did you work with Marie Lucas?
Oh, the regular summer season, you know? Then I left -- my wife came back, and I think I left with my wife and went back to Washington.
What year did you and Rose get married?
1933 at St. Marks Church in New York City. We're Catholic, you know.
Oh.
Did you hear that?
Rose remembers!
No, I mean did you hear that?
Oh, yeah. We'll pick it up. She spoke loudly enough. There was something I want to know. Is your name Rose or is it Rosebud?

I was born Rosebud, and then they changed -- I changed it. All my family called me Bud, and everybody I knew in Washington, D.C., for a long time, called me Bud. That's how Duke Ellington got to calling me Rosebud; he always called me Rosebud.
I know Duke did; I didn't know whether Duke just called you that because he wanted to call you that because you and he were so close, or ...
No, I was born Rosebud, but then when I got to be a little older, I didn't like it -- it sounded too childish, so I stopped everybody from calling me Rosebud,
and they said what's your name, and I'd say Rose.
Everybody but Duke.
But he continued calling me Rosebud.
I know -- even in his book, he called you Rosebud.
Yes, yeah.
Do you remember any of the other musicians who worked with Marie Lucas when you did?
Well, the musicians were Puerto Rican fellows.
Uh huh. Do you remember any of their names?

Well, Frank Marcossi was playing bass. Julio Kavanar, he was playing violin, and one of the best violin players -- we had two violin players over there, the best two violin players in the country -- they came there to Washington and stayed there at the Howard Theatre. Dulivera and Adiosta (phonetic) and we had a trumpet player that was in Washington there for quite awhile playing second trumpet, but the first trumpet, he came from Puerto Rico -- oh, gosh, I can't remember. And we had a french horn, he was the brother of the trumpet player, from Puerto Rico, and Calderone, Cal Deron, the drummer.
Uh huh. Did you play Latin music or popular music? from this country or everything.
Oh, we'd play anything. We play anything

over there. That orchestra we had in there, we had people that came from the downtown orchestra; you know, there used to be a big orchestra in the Rialto Theatre in Washington; they used to come over, you know, to hear our band, because we were used to playing overtures, and they were first class musicians. (unintelligible) (unintelligible) It was not just a bunch of school kids, you know.
So did you and Duke get to be friends at the Howard Theatre?

We got to be friends at the Howard Theatre -- not too much, but he knew about me, you know? He had heard about me when I played in the pit band. So when he sent for me, I was just very happy to go over. Whetsol Wetzel was a trumpet player that talked to Duke -- you know Harry Wetzel? Whetsol? No, Arthur Whetsol, the trumpet player, that talked to Duke, to send for me, you know? So I went over, and I started at the Cotton Club.
How long after you met Duke at the Howard was it before he sent for you? Do you remember?
You have any idea?
I didn't know that you had met him at the Howard Theatre. I don't know nothing about that.

It was quite a bit on, because After the Howard Theatre, he left Washington, you know -- Duke left Washington to go to New York, him and Sonny Greer; they left for New York to play in a small place that was very popular in New York. But

I was not with him then; I was still in Washington. The only time I got with him is just when, like I said before, when he got the show in Zigfield Follies, then he knew he could afford to have me in the band, because he figured he was a different kind of musician and so forth, and he knew my reputation about reading and so forth.

So I joined the band, and we used to play in the Zigfield show at night, and after the show, we would get in two taxicabs and run right over to the Cotton Club and play over there -- and we'd play at the Cotton Club until three o'clock. We had two shows, and he gave me $125 a week, which was a lot of money at that particular time, for playing both at the Zigfield Follies and at the Cotton Club.
So what time did the show start at the Zigfield Follies?
Well, it was regular legit show, like eight o'clock or eight thirty, or something like that.
What time were you through at the Cotton Club?
At the Cotton Club? Three o'clock.
You were through at three.
Three o'clock, yeah.
And you worked from eight to three every night?
Yeah.
Seven nights? Six nights?
Oh, yes indeed. No, we used to be -- we didn't have a night off in New York, huh?
You didn't have a night off?
I can't remember if we got a night off. I think so, it must be -- because in New York there was a law to have a night off somewhere, you know?
Uh huh.
I thiknk we had a night off, but I just don't quite remember -- that was a long time ago.
What year was that? I think I have it written down somewhere, but do you remember what year it was that you went to join Duke in New York?
No, I can't. Do you remember when it was that we had the delicatessan store?
That's okay, it's probably written down someplace. Who was in Duke's band when you joined it?

When I joined Duke Ellington in the Cotton Club, it was Arthur Whetsol, Freddie Wetzel, Phil Jenkins, Cootie Williams, Freddie Guy, a guitar player, and we had Otto Hardwick, Hiwork, saxophone, Johnny Hodges, and Carney, and on the drums was Sonny Greer, and the bass player was that fellow from New Orleans, what's his name?
Wilmon Brough? Wellman Braud?
Yeah, Wellman Braud. Wilman-Brough.
According to Leonard Feather and John Chilton's Johnny Shul-ton's book, you went to New York in either August or
September of 1929 -- one book says August, one book says September, 1929.
I think that's quite right.
Sounds right? Okay. It says you also worked with Bobby Lee's Cotton Pickers.
Oh yeah.
When was that?
Oh gosh. If you ask me about dates, I won't be able to tell you.
Was that before you worked with Duke, or after?
No, that was after; that was after. I worked with Bobby Lee to Philadelphia, to work over there in a nightclub.

So you stayed with Duke when you went to work for the Zigfield Follies and the Cotton Club; you stayed with Duke -- let's see, it says quite a long time, but did you leave for a short time to go with Bobby Lee?
No, no. When I had been with Bobby Lee, I had already finished with Duke.
Oh. Well, how long were you with Duke at first?
Thirteen years.
Oh, this was like, in the forties, then, that you worked with Bobby Lee?
Yeah, I guess so, because I was with
Duke for a long time.
Yeah, it says '29 to '44. How about the White Brothers Band?

The White Brothers was when I was in Washington; that's what I said, when I was in the pit band in there, and I stayed in Washington, and they dissolved the pit band orchestra; then I was for myself. Then I used to work there with the White Brothers; they made a combination of about five musicians to play at Youngstown and Philadelphia and so forth, doing one nighters. I was with the White Brothers Orchestra.
Who else was in that band? How big an orchestra?
Oh, it was nothing but two saxophones, trombone, trumpet, drum and bass player. It was a small band.
Do you remember who any of the musicians were?

huh?

But there was never any difficulty with Duke's band like that? in the South? Except some questions once in a while.
questions.
No, no. I don't think so. Just
Never any legal difficulties?

In some place in Henderson, Texas -- that was a tough town. We were playing a dance for a lot of big people in there, and some of them cowboys and so on, and one of the ladies in there came by and tried to sit down in the same seat as Duke Ellington, you know? Oh, he was scared to 'Cause there was people in the front there, too. And the fellow that was dancing with her was out there in front of the bandstand, and probably said, to himself, "I wonder what my girlfriend is sitting down talking with a nigger".

So Duke was scared, and called for Jack Boyd -- "Jack, take this lady out of here, take her out!'. So by the end of the dance, somebody picked up Tricky's trombone, they picked it up and took it with them. We was getting ready to go on the bus and it was right behind -- I mean, Tricky 's trombone, so they said, "you know, I'm gonna take this trombone with me and I don't care if you tell the police, you know? I don't give a damn about the police in there." He was a big man there in Texas -- an old man, you know? He said, "he didn't give a damn about the police coming." Duke said, "Well, if that's the way you feel about it -- there's the trombone. If you want it, go ahead and take it." That killed him when he said that, and he said, "No, it's all right; I don't want the trombone -- I all just wanted to see was how he was gonna act about it." You know?
That's about the worst one we had. They used to bother me, asking me questions -- like Lawrence Brown used to sit down at the end, did he tell you about that?
I don't think so.

Lawrence Brown used to sit down at the end, and then I was next, then Tricky on the other side; they used to come out and talk and want to find out this and that, and so forth. "What are you?" I'd say, "Sure, I'm white." "Well, what you doing playing with us?" Oh, well, I used to say the same thing I would tell everybody. "This is a big band the man has a good reputation, play for everybody -- kings, queens, everybody, the President and everybody." So ...

They used to go to Brown and ask him questions, too, and Brown would say, "Let's change the seat; you sit down here and I'll sit there." I'd say, "That's all right, it don't make no difference, I'll sit there." I knew what to answer.
It seems like I read someplace, some time, that there were areas where the band would go where they couldn't go to the restaurants, and so you and Jack Boyd would get the food?

Oh, yeah. Oh, we used to go there, me and Jack Boyd used to get it -- in the bus, we used to stop places. Oh, we went someplace, and I went over and sat down, you know, at the regular chair and I asked for what I wanted, but then somebody -- I don't know who -- came back, and they

wouldn't serve them, you know? And so I said, 'Well, if you don't serve them, you don't serve me, either, because I'm with them.' They said they could go back in the kitchen and get it in the kitchen, you know?
So I'd get some food and take it to them; I used to do that all the time down South.

I think -- Barney was telling me about how he was cooking in the baggage car when they had the two cars, one for his traveling and one for the baggage and instruments, and someplace down south, I think he told me, he got a little stove or something, and was cooking in the car, and I think Duke smelled the food and came in and after that Barney said Duke wanted him to do the cooking all the time. Do you remember that?
No, I don't remember. I know he was cooking -- like Taylor, the bass player, he used to cook in the baggage car.
Is that the way everybody ate? I mean, you used the Pullman to sleep in in the south, right? When you stopped in a town, you'd stay in the car, when you weren't on the job.
Yeah ...
So was that the only way to eat, to cook your own food?
No, sometimes you go to the station where they sell it over there, or we send the porter out to serve you
to get something to eat.
Uh huh.
Oh, we had a little trouble, but it didn't mean nothing -- naturally they don't want you to go here, they don't want you to do this or that, but we got away.
Tell me about Tricky Sam. What was he like?
Tricky?
Uh huh. I never knew him.

What he was like? Tricky was a hell of a nice fellow. Only he liked his whiskey, you know, and when he got full of whiskey, you didn't know what he was gonna play! But he was a nice fellow, very nice.
How about Whetsol?

Oh, Whetsol was a quiet fellow, a very quiet fellow. There was not much for him to ... we could find out that he was getting bad because he used to go there and play whatever he had to play, and he was shaking and everything, and could hardly make sense. We start finding out, when it was getting awful bad, he'd get very nervous. And I never did realize what he died of.
I don't know, either.
I know I heard something that his hair turned white completely.
How about Freddie Guy?
Freddy Guy; oh well, he and Duke and

Sonny used to argue a lot. Freddy Guy used to hit would be saying what he would do and this and that. But they argued with Duke on everything -- but nothing amounted to anything. But Sonny Greer and Duke -- they used to call each other such things, but there wasn't nothing to it.
Sonny used to claim he discovered Duke.
Well, I don't know about that; I don't know about that.
Brooks Kerr, a young man in New York, asked me to ask you about Shep Allen.
Shep Allen? He was the manager of the Howard Theatre. I imagine he is still there, I don't know.
And then Brooks said Hernandez, who was a violinist.
He's a violinist?
A violinist named Hernandez.
I don't know about that.
Okay. And a drummer named Cutie Perkins?
I don't know that, either.
I don't know who these people are -- I didn't know who any of them were, but Brooks told me that when I talked to you that I should ask you, because these
might be people that you might remember, I guess, from Washington.
Well, I knew Shep Allen, but no, I don't know these other fellows.
Okay. I understand from Barry Ulanov's "Ko-Ko" book that Ceecea came from an opera Duke was writing called "Bula".
I didn't hear you.
I say I read in Barry Ulanov's book that the piece "Ko-Ko" came from an opera Duke was writing that he called "Bula". Do you remember Bula?
No, I don't know anything about that.
And he said that when he wrote "Black, Brown and Beige," he took some of the material that he was planning to use in "Bula," and put it in "Black, Brown and Beige."
Well, I don't know about that. No, I don't know a thing about that.
Because that would've been what? The 1943 concert, I think.
How about Billy Strayhorn? You were there when he came in to the band, right?
Oh, yeah. We got Strayhorn from Pittsburgh -- he's from Pittsburgh -- he came in the band, oh, I think he was writing something for Duke, and I arranged
something, and he liked it, so I guess he hired him them. He was a good musician -- very good. He got everything that Duke had, as far as arranging and so forth. And more.
Do you think that they learned from each other, or do you think that Billy learned from Duke, or ...

No, Strayhorn learned. He already knew about it -- by looking at somebody's scores, sometimes, he learned a lot and he started writing just like Duke Ellington. I'm talking about his chords score and so forth.

I've heard some people in the band say that they couldn't tell them apart, from what they wrote; they couldn't tell whose music they were playing -- Duke's Strayhorn's or Strayhorn's. And other people say they could tell the difference. How about you?
Oh, sure. Strayhorn's was a little more sweeter, more sweet music than anything else -- you could tell in a way he uses his phrases in the music, you know, you could tell it was Strayhorn. Strayhorn.

How about the way they communicated? I mean when they worked on something together, they seemed to be on the same wavelength -- the that one would know what the other was writing, and they could do a few; one would do a few bars and the next one would do a few bars, and they all flowed smoothly.
Well, I don't know about that. What

they did together and so forth; maybe, you know, in their home or something -- in Duke Ellington's home or somewhere, but I don't know anything about that. For what he had to write for the band, Duke Ellington didn't have to look for nobody to tell him nothing -- I mean for his band.
Did you work with him, I think you did, didn't you -- on Anatomy of a Murder? Were you in Los Angeles when they were writing that?
I don't think so.
Tom Waley was here. Maybe he did the extraction. Because I can't remember whether ... that would be 1959, I think. You were probably out with Harry James.
No, I don't know anything about that.
Were you with Harry James in 1959?
Yes. Yes. He was with Harry James for 10 years.
You left Duke in 1944, is that right?
That's right.
That is right.
What -- you were out here and didn't want to travel any more, is that why?
That's right.
And, see, Harry James' base was here; Duke Ellington's base was in New York.
How this thing came out -- we were at

the Cotton Club, and I asked Duke to give me some money to pay for the home, the balance on my home, which was about $3,000 owed on the home. I said, "Would you loan me that money and take it out of my salary?" Oh, he swore that he didn't have the money, and this and the other and so forth, and at that time, he had a good check from that song, between Harry James and Duke and Harry James Hodges, and somebody else, I forgot the name of it now -- but he got a pretty good amount of money.

So I said, "Well, I tell you what I'll do. I might as well go ahead and quit" -- and Harry James called me up at the Cotton Club and they wanted to know if I could come in their band. I said, "Well, I guess so" -- especially since I wanted to come to California, because I used to come to California to see her once a year. So I wanted to go home, you know? I didn't want to keep on the road any more, and then I went to Harry James, and he offered me a good salary, so I quit.

"Oh, you can't do that." And I said, "Don't tell me what I can quit do" -- so he sent me my contract, and I showed it to him, and he I said, "Listen, how about me buying that contract back from Harry James?" I said, "No, I don't want for you to do that; you can't to it anyhow, because I'm going anyhow." He offered me money; he said, "I offer you what you ask me for, and besides, I send Rose $50 every week if you stay" -- and I said, 'I can't do that'. Oh, he was
hot about that.
You mentioned off the tape that sometimes you and Duke disagreed, right?
Disagreed about what?
You didn't mention what; you just said that sometimes you would have disagreements, most of the time you got along -- but sometimes you didn't get along. Right?

Well, I disagreed with him a lot of times -- the department in the band, about certain guys with the dope business, you know? Because I say, 'If ever the band come in here, well, I'm gonna tell who is using the dope in the band. I ain't going to jail.' Oh, he couldn't take that; he wouldn't see that at all.
So we disagreed on that, and the little trumpet player -- what was his name -- the little dark boy ...
Ray Nance?
No, no. Not Ray Nance.
Freddie Jenkins?
No, no.
Oh, I know who you mean. The one who had the family.
Well, anyhow -- if he goes bad, full of dope or something like that ...
Willie Cook?

Yeah. He wouldn't play nothing; he'd put his trumpet in his lap and wouldn't play. I used to look back at him like I wanted to kill him, you know? So I just walked away from the bandstand and I'd go outside on the street someplace; I would walk around to get myself together.
But that's the only time I disagreed -- he didn't know what to do.
What did he say when you objected to that?

Oh, he never said nothing to me. He'd say, 'What's the matter?' and I'd say, 'You know what it is. How can you stand all that stuff like that?' But he knew how he was, even with the tenor player -- what was his name?
Paul Gonsalves?

Yeah, Paul. He's sleeping out there in front of the public, sleeping and so forth like that -- Oh, he take a lot of things. (Unintelligible) how can you take all that? I don't know. I guess he figured he couldn't get anybody like him.
But Paul was a beautiful player when he was awake and playing.
Huh?
Paul played beautifully.
Oh, he was a good man, but he also got into that dope business, you know. God bless him, he died.
So you went ahead and left Duke, and you went with Harry James?
Yeah. I played seven years with Harry James.
Ten years!
No, not exactly ten, baby.
You were with Harry James and you left him and went back to Duke, and then you went back to Harry James again -- so all together, it was 10 years.
Just call it say ten then, yes.
But the first time, it was seven years, and then you left. So did Harry travel much when you were with him, during those seven years?
Oh, my Lord, yes. He used to do a lot of one nighters.
More than Duke?
He used to do a lot of one nighters.
But you see, he'd always come back to California, so Juan would be home.
We did a lot of recording, but mostly one nighters -- on bus, too.
Was it more traveling than Duke?
Well, no, because Duke was all year round -- Duke traveled the whole year round, he never stopped; he'd say, 'I don't stop; I keep on going.'
Harry James had that radio program here -- the Chesterfield thing, wasn't it?
It was the Coca Cola thing.
Was it every day, or three days a week? How often was it?
No, once a week, I think.
It was with Dinah Shore.
So how did you feel musically from going from Duke Ellington to Harry James?
Well, it was altogether different. Harry James was more on the commercial side, you know.
But Harry played your numbers, didn't he?
He tried, but he used to have an arrangement on Perdido and Caravan. He had an arrangement, which featured me in front of the bandstand, and I wrote a tune later on -- I forgot the name.
"You Can't Have Your Cake, and Eat It Too."
Yeah, he did that; he had an arrangement made with that.
Yeah, and Willie Smith sang.
Yeah. Oh, he did some things of mine, yes.
When did you write that? "You Can't Have Your Cake and Eat It Too?"
Oh, that was a long time ago. I was in New York. He had an arrangement on that, and Willie Smith sang the arrangement and one record that I made, Willie sang the lyrics on that.
Who did the arrangements on your tunes in Harry's band?
In Harry's band, Thompson -- what was his first name?
All I knew him by was Thompson.
Thompson was a very good arranger. He was from Dallas, Texas.
Was Willie in the band when you got there, or did he come in afterward?

No, Duke and Willie came in the band while we was in Jersey at that club outside of Newark; he came in the band -- he was in Chicago then, and Harry asked me to call him, and I called him and talked to him, and I said 'Harry wanted for you to come in the band,' and he said okay. So he got him, and he joined there in Jersey in this club we were playing at.
Meadowbrook.
Meadowbrook, yeah.
But you knew Willie before?
Oh, yeah, yeah. I had known Willie since he was with Jimmy Lunceford.
Did you meet him when you were in Washington or New York?
Wherever they were playing, or something; he was a good saxaphone player.
And a nice person, I remember. I knew him when he was with Duke's band.
Yes, he was a very good player.

Do you remember any incidents when Willie was in Harry's band? I remember the one that Willie told me about traveling in the south, but -- the fact that some southerners would know that Willie was really colored -- was there ever any incident where anybody tried to make any trouble because he was playing with a white band?
Oh, that was down south somewhere, when we got back together before.
Did it happen often?
I'm talking about when we already recorded.

When we talked about Duke's band -- I'm talking about Willie in Harry James' band. Because I remember that Willie told me about how one time they came looking for him because they heard they were coming to town and they had laws against mixed bands.
Oh, that was down South, yes.
Yeah, down South. Did that happen often? I remember one time Willie told me.
(unintelligible)
No, I don't know about any more.
And didn't Harry James refuse to play for segregated audiences down south? Do you remember?
No, I don't know anything about that.
I think he did one time, Juan.
Well, I don't remember.
How was Harry to work for?
Oh, he was all right.
Wonderful.
Sometimes he was tough, you know, because he likes everything like it should be, you know? He's a good musician.
He had deportment in his band.

Oh, he couldn't stand too much of that. But a very good man. If you do your work, he's all right. I had a little trouble with him one time; I almost fought him, too. We were playing a dance and he called for a tune that we hadn't played for a long, long time and I didn't have a part, so the other trombone said, 'I believe I got a part in here.' He got me a part, and at the end, we found out that the part he gave me was a french horn part; it wasn't a trombone part, and naturally, when we started playing the tune, the place where they had three trombones playing something -- I was playing the wrong thing. I was playing the wrong thing, you know, so right there where we

playing, he said it's G, and I said, 'No, that it was G natural -- oh, I don't know whatever happened, but he was hollering at me and I was hollering at him, while the people were dancing and everything.

I said, 'Look here,' and I showed him the part, so he hollered at me and after we got through to intermission, he went to his dressing room and I had my mouthpiece in, you know, and I got it out of the trombone, in case he tried to do anything. I went over there and took the part with me, and I said, 'Here it is.' I said, 'Harry, you're wrong', and you was hollering at me about the part and I'm showing you that you was wrong, and he finally said, 'You're right. I'm sorry, Juan. Have a drink with me.' And he took the bottle, because he always had a bottle with him all the time in the dressing room. So I said, 'Okay' -- I didn't drink but I took a drink.
Well, that's good that he was able to admit he was wrong.
Oh, sure.

Nice guy. Because I know when they went down south, and he's from the South, you know. A lot of people think he's Jewish, you know, but he's from the south, and he said he was ashamed to be from the South after that first incident with Willie Smith, you know?
Uh huh.
Nice guy. And Betty Benny was as nice as
he was. He used to have a Christmas party for the band every year, and everybody in the band was invited, and it was just lovely.
You made more money with Harry than with Duke, is that right?
Oh, when I first went in the band, yeah.
So was Harry's band generally better paid than Duke's, as far as you know?
Better what?
Was Harry's band better paid than Duke's band, as a whole, do you know?

Oh, no, I don't think so. Duke always had, like, Johnny Hodges, Harry Carney -- Lawrence, but Lawrence never made as much money as Johnny or Harry Carney made, and I guess that's about all. Maybe a couple other guys -- I don't know how much they made, but that's the only one that really made money in the band.
But Duke was willing to pay you a lot more money when he thought he was going to lose you, right?
Oh, he offered me money.
Duke would pay as much as he had to pay, usually. Was it in Harry's band that you met Louis Belson? Or did you know him before?
Wait a minute, let's see ...
It was in Harry's band.

He was in Harry's band. That's when Duke Ellington was there at that gambling place -- what is it -- Las Vegas. I used to go and see him, I was with Harry James in one club and Duke was at another club, so I used to go there between intermissions, and he asked me to see if I could get -- what's his name -- Louis. He asked about me, to get me, and I said 'Well, how about Willie Smith too?' So the three of us, we went with Duke Ellington.
So Duke asked you first, and then he asked you to get Louis and then you asked him about Willie? I never knew how that happened, whether Duke just went and took all three of you at once, or what.
No, it wasn't that way. Juan got Louis and Willie to go with him. They didn't want to go at first; They had good jobs and were alreadt working.
Oh, Harry he was mad at me.
Yeah, I think Duke makes some comments about that in his book.
He did.
Yeah, I'm trying to find it.
He said he really didn't steal Juan from Harry because Juan was with him first.
Yeah, right. Harry stole Juan from him, so he was just stealing him back.
Yeah.
But you didn't really fell like
you were stolen, did you?
For Duke?
You didn't feel that Harry stole you, did you?
No. Juan wanted to come to California.

Yeah, I wanted to come to California, because I hadn't been here. I used to come here, like I say before, I used to come here just once a year, you know, for Christmas, and I knew the band was coming this way, so I told Duke, "I was going out for six weeks. For six weeks, I'd be out here in California." At one time, I came over here, and Harry had at a concert in Philadelphia, and my six weeks was not up, so he called me up, and he said, "How about you coming over to Philadelphia? I have to have you there for a concert". And I said, "But my six weeks is not up yet. How am I going to get there?" He said, "Well, just pay for the ticket and I'll pay you ahead of time."

When I went over there, when I went to Philadelphia to play the concert, that particular night, that I got there -- I used to get paid on Thursday night, and on Thursday night, here comes the manager paying off, and he paid me for one day for the concert and I said, "No, you got to pay me for the whole week. I work for Duke Ellington, and work or don't work, I get paid every week", which I did. If they don't play, that's their business. I get my money. I'd go to what's his

name, and I'd say, 'Give me my money', and I'd say, 'You got to give me my money; I can't get paid for just one day. After all, you sent for me to come to Philadelphia, and I was having a nice time with my family, so I think I deserve to get paid'.
So he told the manager to pay me off.
Was Al Celley the manager then?
Yeah.
Al Celley used to not pay unless he had to.
Oh ...
So then you were back with Duke. Did you have any idea what a difference Louie was going to make with the band?
Oh, sure; I was sure he was going to make it. Oh, the band was crazy about Louie.

I can remember when he first came in, how the band used to look so bored during a drum solo or just bored most of the time, and then when Louie came in, they all turned around and watched and applauded, and stood up.
Oh, he was great. He was learning doing arrangements from Strayhorn, you know? He used to ask questions of Strayhorn about arranging.
Louie Bellson is a fine man.
Yeah, he certainly is.
A fine man.

I remember in the band bus-- how I'd ridden, different it was from the times before when I read, that when Louie was there, he and Wendell used to ride in the back of the bus with a radio playing classical music, and I never heard classical music on the band bus before that. But Louie was so interested in so many kinds of music.
Well, Juan introduced Louie and Pearl.
Oh, I thought it was you?
No, I was home. I knew both of them; Pearl and I were friends.

No, we was at the Howard Theatre, and Pearl was getting ready to start working in a white club there, and she happened to be across the street from the stage -- that's where everybody eat, and so forth, and Louie was coming out, and I said, "Louie, come here, I want for you to meet Pearl Bailey." "Pearl Bailey?" He said, "Well, naturally." He said I'm opening tonight at the club so and so, and I wish you'd bring Louie with you tonight after you get through." I said, "Sure" and we went over there, and Pearl opened champagne and everything.

And that night, we went to a place uptown, in Georgetown, to a place where they had food, and we ate, and Pearl Bailey had a Buick, was driving a Buick, and we was living downtown -- Louie and me, we were living downtown, so I said, "I got to go now", so she said, "Well, take my car".

So I took the car and went to the hotel, and Louie went with Pearl. The next morning, Pearl called and said, "Juan, do you know what happened? He asked me to marry him". And they went to London (1943) and everything like that.
Oh, I remember, yeah.
That's where they got married, in London.
Yeah.
And he's the same Louie Bellson today.
Right away, he had made a wedding ring, with all diamonds and everything. (1943)
Yeah, I remember when they got married.
They really got together, all right.
It's been a long time, too.
Twenty some years now.
How about you? You married, too? You're still married, huh?
No.
But you were married.
I was married, but I'm not any more.
Oh, no more?
No more. No. By myself.
So it was not too long after that that Louie left Duke, right? Because he and Pearl didn't want to be separated, right?
So it was shortly after they got married -- how long was it? I don't remember, but after they got married, then Louie left him, right?
Oh, naturally. Yeah, Louie left him.
And went with Pearl.
Yeah, went with Pearl.

Then there was that period when they did a tour together, when they worked at the Paramount downtown here and the Paramount in San Fransico -- Pearl, and Duke's band, and then that way, Louie played in Duke's band for a little while again. That was not too long, though, what was it -- about a year or so after they got married?
Not too long. About a year, I imagine.
Yeah, because Duke always said that Pearl stole his drummer.
So, then you were back with Duke, for how long? I've forgotten now.

When I went back, I went back for almost three years. Willie had gone because Willie couldn't take it. He couldn't take it no more. I had to beg him to stay with the band, and all this. I forgot what the trouble was that he disliked about it -- the band or something, so he left the band and Louie left, too.
I think you were back with Duke for quite awhile there, after you went back the second time, Juan.

Because you didn't come home until after we moved in to this house -- 'cause when you left, we were on Hobart Blvd. -- and do you remember? You came home after we were in this house, so the last time you went with Duke, you were back there quite a while. Do you remember now?
Uh huh.
Yeah ...
You had that beautiful big house on Hobart Blvd. You had to sell it when the freeway came through?
Yeah. The freeway came right through the living room.
We turned it into apartments, you know.
It seems like you did that, yeah.
Yeah, we had five apartments over there -- we had four apartments in our house.
I remember it was a wonderful big house.
Oh, it was a beautiful home, a beautiful home. The man we bought it from was one of the founders of the Richfield Oil Company, so that answers all questions.
Yeah.
A wonderful man. Talked to me an awful lot.
What was his name?
What was that man's name, Juan?
You know I don't remember names.
He was Scottish.
Well, if you remember later on, we can just put it in.

Yeah, he was Scottish, and he told me so much about business and how to do it. He paid people six months at a time, you know, and the people who built that house, he brought from Scotland to build the house, and paid them room and board while they were here, and he would pay his gardener and the people who worked for him, like six months at a time, and he told me, he said, 'I have a gardener and I have paid him in advance, so he will stay with you until his time is up'.
How wonderful ...

And he said, 'We have had some trash in the back yard, and he'll clean that all out, and he sent a man over to clean the house up. And we had a pantry, and there was a little crack in one of the windows, and he had that fixed. Oh, I'm trying to think of that man's name, but he and his wife both are very, very nice people. Juan and I were young, you know, and we didn't know anything about real estate, and we told him an awful lot. He really taught me a lot.
When you went back with Duke, did
you continue to write?
No. I haven't written a thing no more since I left Duke; I haven't wrote anything.
Why?
I don't know.
I think Juan got disgusted in the way that he had been treated, you know, in the music business -- you know what I mean?
And I am still disgusted with them. Oh, they treat you down right they treat you so badly -- ain't no way you can go there and fight those people.
Well, the only way you could do it is to write something new and then deal with other, with different people.
And then, right after that, they started bringing in the different kind of music ...
Rock and roll.
Rock and roll, and this and the other, and I couldn't write that stuff. So I just didn't bother, so I haven't written a thing in years, just like I haven't touched my trombone in about 10 years.
And they haven't done a thing with 'Gypsy Without a Song,' and that's the most beautiful tune that you've ever heard.
She must have heard it.
Yeah.
But, see, Juan got disgusted.
Didn't you write something for Louie's first record date?
Who?
Louie Bellson's first record date?
Yes. On Hobart Boulevard, but I've forgotten what it was now.
I've got the record.
I can't remember.

Was that Blanche -- no, that was Louie's tune. I remember that it was a 10 inch LP and it was done on Capital -- but I remember Duke and Strayhorn played on the thing and Duke was there at that date. You were there, too, but were you playing? It seems like one of the tunes on Capital was yours.

Yeah.

Yeah, Dorothy Dandridge, Herbie. Did Cab Calloway work there? No. I don't know ...

How about who were some of the dancers -- Key Louise Franklin, Alice Teed. Do you remember that the program changed a lot? I heard that every week the show would change some; that they would take old numbers out and put new numbers in.

Well, they tried to make a real -- all the time, they was trying to, the show itself -- not the music so much, but the show itself; they would keep trying to improve it, because more people were interested.
(Unintelligible)
to get more money to back it up because they were thinking wanted to take at that time of taking it to New York. it to New York at that time
Uh huh. And I understand that John Garfield was one of the people who backed it. Do you remember that?
No, I don't. I don't remember, but there was quite a few people in there that was interested in that show. He was a good, nice actor. A Wonderful Smith.
A Wonderful Smith, yes. I understand he is a minister now.
He is?
That's what someone told me. Remember "Pot, Pan and Skillet"?
Oh, yeah, sure. I remember especially him.
And Ivy le Anderson? How about Ivy le Anderson?

Oh, she was wonderful; she was She was a hell of a gambler-- wonderful. A She used to keep some of the boys broke, she was good in gambling, and in poker. She stayed day and there at night gambling; it didn't make any difference to her.
How about Duke's taste in singers? I mean the singers he'd pick; Ivy le you liked very much -- but did you like all of the singers that he picked?
What?
What did you think of the singers

Well, the only one I can remember was in the show "Jump for Joy", I don't know who hired her, Dorothy Dandridge. Duke didn't have nothing to do with that. But Ivie Anderson, we got her in Chicago. Oh yeah, whatever she did, she was suffering with asthma, you know? And she could hardly -- sometimes they used to tell me that down South, she had it so bad, she would have to go out on the street to get some air because she's couldn't hardly breathe, but she could be feeling bad right now on the stage and go there and sing, and you couldn't tell she had asthma. She was terrific.
You remember Marie Cole.
Marie Cole?
Yeah, when she sang with Duke?
When she sang with the band; you remember Marie used to sing with the band.
Was with our band?
Certainly.
Her name was Marie Ellington, then, right?
Unh huh ...
She and two other girls.
Yeah, Joy, Cheryl and Kay Davis.
That's right.
Oh, I remember Kay Davis and Cheryl -- she's around here somewhere.
No, they weren't in that show. Kay joined the band later on.
Like I said before, there's not much I can say about "Jump for Joy", what happened or anything like that.
I see, okay. And you don't remember working on any of the music for it?
No, no.
Strayhorn was around then, and Duke and Strayhorn were staying at the -- I guess the whole band was staying at the Dunbar Hotel.
Yeah.
I know they told me that Duke and Strayhorn were working on the music for it at the Dunbar right up until the time it opened.
