Rose reminded us that there was a big event in Puerto Rico honoring your uncle a few years ago. Tell me about that.
Oh, yeah, that was in '69. They were honoring my uncle since he was such a hell of a musician, and I went there in '69, after 44 years of not having been to

Puerto Rico, since I left Puerto Rico. And I went over there, and the first thing was they said a Mass at about eight o'clock in the morning for him, and then we went to, from there, we went to the street where he was born, where my uncle was born, Cruz Cruise Street, like cross, you know? Cruz Cruise Street, number 31, and they called it black -- Manuel Tizol was born there, and I was raised right there, because I was born right there in the house, and I was raised right there with my family.
And, from there, then we went to the City Hall which, I think, is in one of those pictures in there of City Hall. See it there? There's a picture of when we were at City Hall.
Oh, I see -- with all those people.
Those are members of the family?

Yeah, those are my nieces and their husbands and their children. They were at City Hall, and there was talk and a piano player played a lot of Spanish dancers, and Puerto Rican dancers. And they had something to eat and so forth.

And that night, the Municipal Band was there with a different leader then, was giving a concert in the Plaza where we used to give concerts all the time; they gave a concert, and it was just raining like the devil, and they couldn't do it. And the leader said they had prepared a very good program, but it was just so that they couldn't do it because it rained so terrible.
It was like a holiday, you know? Honoring him.

And that was the end of that. From there, me and my niece and the family went to a nightclub to eat some of that rice with shrimp and all that business. So from there, they took me back to the hotel where we were staying.
We started it with an eight o'clock Mass, didn't we?
Yeah, I told her that.
Yeah, the whole day was dedicated to him.
Oh, he was a wonderful man, a wonderful man.
His name wasn't Manuel -- it was Manola.
Well, they called him Manola, but his name was Manuel.
Manuel? M-a-n-u-e-l?
That's his name -- Manuel, yeah.
Manola is a affectionate nickname for Manuel.
Oh, really?
Yeah.
I never knew that before.
So that was about the end of the trip. I stayed about nine days there and I came back.
They must have been happy to see you, undoubtedly.

Oh, my Lord, yes; my family. Yeah, they gave me -- that Sunday I got in, we went to my cousin's house and they threw a little affair there, you know; invited a few friends; had a couple of musicians that brought played their flutes and they were playing. Oh, yes, and they had a big table with all kinds of Puerto Rican food, you know? Pastelles and everything!
Well, you're a famous man, and to finally come back to your country must have been very exciting for you.
Oh, wonderful. Wonderful.
So the celebration was partly for you, too, then, wasn't it?
Oh, yes.
What year did your uncle die?
Oh, I don't know about that. I can't keep track of dates.
Okay. Was it very long before this?
Oh yes. He has four daughters and one boy. They were all married with children.
Makes It was a big family. Rose, you mentioned that you remembered the name of the man we were talking about yesterday, that who bought your house on Hobart Boulevard from.
Mr. Simington.
Do you remember his first name?
No, I don't. I never knew his first name; I used to call him Mr. Simington all the time. Because he was quite a settled man, and at that time we were kind of young, you know.

Uh huh. You were mentioning earlier on the other tape about the situation where you helped Willie and how grateful he was always, to you. Were you around the band when Johnny Hodges kind of befriended Paul Gonzalves and sort of helped him all the time and looked out for him?
No, I don't know about that.

Because sometimes when Paul didn't have any money, Johnny would see to it that he did and Johnny would feed him, and I remember once, Al Selle was so disgusted with Paul that when they got in-to the airport in Los Angeles, everybody took cabs or made some arrangements to get to the hotel, and Selle knew that Paul Gonzalves didn't have any money, so Selle just went off and left him. And Johnny realized that just as he was about to get in a cab -- because Paul told me this -- that Paul had no way of getting there, and everybody was going off and leaving him, especially Selle. He asked Selle for cabfare and Selle said, 'I'm not giving you any money'1.
So Johnny got a cab and took Paul to the hotel. And
he was always watching out for him like that.
Wasn't he wonderful?

Yeah. I know when Johnny died, Sam Woodward was living here in Los Angeles, and I saw Sam on the street the day I heard about Johnny, and so I pulled up and told Sam the news, and Sam started to cry and he said, 'With the General gone, who's gonna look after Max?', because Paul always needed somebody to kind of look out for him.
Uh huh. And he wasn't long afterwards.
Not much longer.
No. Johnny was a lovely man.
He had a big heart.
And Jewel is nice, too. I hear from her now and then; she calls me.
Were there a lot of close friendships in the band or not? I mean the people in the band ... did they --
Real close friends, Juan. Were there many close friends in Duke's band?
Well, I think everybody was good friends to each other.
They all got along nicely.
But later on, a lot of people didn't. Like in the late sixties ...
Oh, yeah. But see, that was a little
different group all together.

See, I was good friends with all the saxophone players and all the trumpet players, and I know I was all right with Lawrence Brown. The only one was the one trombone player they had, the one after Tricky -- after Tricky died, we got this trombone player, he was a plunger man, but some of the parts in there he couldn't handle and I got into little arguments with him and I told him he couldn't play the parts -- he couldn't blow the horn. I mean, he could blow the horn, but still, he couldn't read well.
So I got into little arguments with him, but that was not too much to it.
But in Duke's old group, Everybody in Duke's band was a gentleman. Weren't they, Juan? Cootie and all those guys, you know. Everybody. Nobody drank.
That's right. We had a time there when nobody drank except Sonny Greer.
Sonny Greer.
And Otto, I think. Sonny Greer and Otto.
They were the only ones in the band who drank.
And later, Barney Bobbie was drinking.
Harry?
Harry didn't drink.
But I mean later, when I was out of
there.
But he didn't use to drink.
Because I could tell Harry when he was drinking, because he was tired and he didn't play.
Cootie didn't drink until later.
Yeah, but they tell me Cootie was drinking pretty heavy later on.

I never saw Cootie drink too much, but I used to see Harry put it away; drink out of the bottle and then get on the road and drive the car and, I don't know how he did it -- because I don't think he ever had an accident.

It's a wonder he didn't get in to an accident driving Duke somewhere on the road to different towns, and after the dances, because he'd want to go to town, and they told me that Harry would really step on the gas, too.

Oh, yeah; he did. He did. He would go -- and he and Duke would brag about how they did 90 miles an hour and they'd beat the band bus. But on the band bus, the people would sleep, and then sometimes in the car Duke would sleep. But Harry would stay awake on 500-mile trips. It was amazing.
Yep.
Now how about Harry Carney? What kind of a person was he?
What about him?
Yeah, tell me about Harry Carney; about working with him.
Well, you know, Harry was a good man -- with his horn and so forth. You can't beat him, that's all there is to it.
And he was a nice guy.
He was the only baritone player.
And he was nice, wasn't he, Juan?
Oh, yes sir. Harry was always a nice fellow.
His parents were nice, too. They were very nice to us when we went to Boston.
I met his mother when I was in Boston.

Do you remember when they used to feed -- his mother used to have the whole band down there on Saturday, and she'd have Boston baked beans and codfish cakes and Boston brown bread. Oh, delicious, and sometimes hot rolls.
Her name was Jenny?
Yeah.

On the whole, we had a pretty good bunch of boys all the time, outside of the couple who went go for the dope. Like the trumpet player, what's his name? Ray Nance. Ray Nance could always play his part.
And he never did bother nobody.
And he could sing and he could play his part, and he stayed right near the bandstand and you couldn't hear his voice for nothing.
He didn't bother nobody. Don't care how high he got, he never bothered anybody.
Ray seemed to be different; he seemed to not really interfere with anybody.
He didn't.
Not like the other people who sort of wiped out.
Yeah. He used to call me a roommate.
Yes, he was an amazing talent; he could do so many things so well.
Oh, yes, he was very good.

He was a good musician. Improvised like mad on that fiddle, or the trumpet. For instance, what was that thing he played -- the A Train; that solo he did on A Train -- that was his own solo. That was not reading; that was improvised; he did that chorus himself.
It was so beautiful, too. How about Ben Webster?
Oh, he was a good musician, too. I liked his work. Even when he was stoned and everything.
He liked Juan, too. He used to give Juan his money. Then he'd get drunk and come back and get it back little by little. But he was very nice to Juan.
Yeah, Ben was a very sweet, gentle person when he didn't take a drink. He was a completely different person when he was drinking, because he would get kind of fierce.
Oh yeah, he'd come to me, he said, "I'm gonna come and tell everybody something tonight, but I don't mean you.
Once he said to me, "Do I scare you?" and I said, "No, did you want to?" and he said, "Yes!".
When he was kind of high or drunk, you had to watch so you didn't hurt his feelings, because he was strong, you know? Oh, he'd put his fist in your face in a minute.
He got in to a lot of fights?
Oh, I guess he had some with the fellows in the band.
I heard he had a bad temper when he got drunk and he would break up places. But I never heard of him ever hurting anybody, even when he was drinking.
No, he never hurt anybody. If he did, he did it outside where nobody knew anything about it; you know what I mean.
Uh huh.
But he'd just come and start cursing and carrying on and nobody would say anything to him, and he'd
go along to bed and mind his business, you know? And then wake up the next morning and say he was sorry and all that, you know -- but he was a sweet kind of a person, you know?
Uh huh. I thought so when I knew him.
Yeah. A terrific musician.

He got interested in photography later on, too, and he took some great pictures. Every once in awhile, he would -- he used to send me pictures. He took a picture of me up at the Monterey Jazz Festival and sent me a copy once -- one of the best pictures I ever saw.
Yeah?
Yeah. He had a lot of talent in a lot of ways. How about Toby Hardwick? Hardwood?
That's another fellow; he didn't bother anybody. He liked his whiskey.

He was sometimes, what -- out of the band because he drank too much, or what? Lawrence told me that when he was hired, Toby was out of the band for awhile. Why was Toby out of the band? Was it is health, or what?
I think he was sick.
I don't know; I don't remember that.
He used to have trouble with asthma, too, remember, Juan?
I don't know; I don't remember that.
He had trouble with it -- I'm sure it was asthma, yes, because Gladys used to have to work on him some nights. He used to have trouble with asthma. And that whiskey didn't do it any good, you know?

Lawrence told me the reason he happened to mentioned that was that, when he joined the band, there were 12 people here working, and Lawrence would have made 13, and Duke wouldn't let Lawrence play until Toby came back and made 14, because Duke didn't want 13 people in the band -- or at least, that was what he told Lawrence; he said it would be bad luck. Remember that? Lawrence said he went all the way across the country before he got to play; he said Duke wouldn't let him play until Toby came back, and so he waited, I don't know, for three weeks or something.
I don't remember a thing about that.
Do you remember Duke being superstitious?
Oh, well, he is superstitious. He admitted that he was superstitious.
Do you remember when he was superstitious? Do you remember any of the superstitions that Duke had?
Well, he used to say never come in his dressing room eating peanuts or something like that.
That was bad luck, huh?
And if you see a button, if you dropped a button in there, he would never like to see a button that somebody dropped on the stage there, or either in his dressing room. He didn't like that.
Or if a button came off his clothes, he wouldn't want it no more.
He didn't want the clothes any more?
He didn't want the button any more.

Somebody said he would give away a coat that had lost a button, because it was bad luck to have that coat any more, and you couldn't sew another button on. I never saw that; I saw other superstitions he had, but I never saw that one.

I know once he had put all the telegrams he received, the congratulatory telegrams he got at an opening, and he'd put them up around his mirror and some of them were from very famous people, so when the engagement was over and he was packing up his stuff, and the valet was packing his clothes, I started to take the telegrams down; I thought he might want to keep them, and he said, 'No, don't touch those -- leave them there', and I said, 'Why?' and he said, 'It's bad luck to take down your opening night telegrams'. I said, 'You mean you're gonna go on to the next town and just leave those there for somebody else?' And he said, 'I don't care
Yeah, he was very superstitious -- no question about that.
Do you remember any other superstitions he had? Did they ever affect his music? Did he worry about anything about numbers in his music?

No, I don't think so. When he wanted to write something, he made up his mind he was going to write it and he'd go and write it. He'd write even on the way down to his house to the club on the taxicab, he would sketch something.
And he could go to sleep just like that. You'd say, 'Duke?' and that was now, and then the next minute, you'd say, 'Duke?' and he'd be sleeping and snoring up a storm.

Oh, he could sleep in the summer time in one of those Pullmans, and we wouldn't have no -- and we'd be parked where they kept the cars, and that was hot. Those Pullmans were as hot as they could be, and Duke would sleep in there with a wool blanket on top of him, and (water) on his chest. He could sleep ... I mean, snore? Oh!
I know Duke liked it hot; he always liked the hotels very hot, and he hated air conditioning.
Oh, he liked a lot of heat in there.
Oh, he didn't like no drafts. He would always say, "that" to shut the door, you know. But he had his good faults, too, God rest his soul.
Yeah? How about when he would steal music from himself?
What do you mean?

When he would have to get a piece of music finished, and he'd come to the end of an idea and he would go back to some other thing he had written and take some of that and put it back in to the new piece. Did you ever see him do that?
Well, he changed around a lot of stuff; out of one composition, he made three compositions.
And sometimes he would take an old one, take an old one and ...

Like -- da da da, da da -- oh, he made ("Once in a While") ("I let a Song Go Out of My Heart") that up. Da, da, da .. he did that. And I forgot what other one, but he would steal one to the other, and change it around. And make a tunes out of it.
Uh huh, and rename it. Lots of times he's rename them, right?
Huh?
Lots of times he'd change the names, and other times he just took a piece of an old number and put it in a new number.
Oh, he'd steal like mad, no question about it. He'd steal from himself!
I know once he said to me, 'Why shouldn't I? Everybody else steals from me, so certainly I ought to be able to!'
Uh huh.
Do you remember any other tunes that he ...
No, no. Right now, I can't get things out; I don't know why. My mind is not working right; I can't remember things.
We didn't talk about Cootie very much; how about Cootie?

Well, Cootie was a quiet fellow; he was not a troublemaker. Of course, he used to fool around with Ivy; he used to fool around -- well, I guess you heard about that anyhow. He used to fool around with Ivy, but it didn't last long. Because they got in to a little trouble one time in the Pullman, and he started to grab one of those hatchets out there in the Pullman -- but nothing ever happened too strong.

No, he was a very nice fellow and kept to himself; he didn't bother nobody. He played his part the best way he could, and that was all -- take his solos. Because one time Cootie was a terrific swing man, you know? When he first came in the band; oh, he could swing any tune. As far as the trumpet section was concerned. Is it true that since I have
been in California, that he had tuberculosis?
I believe he did.
But he got well, all right.
I think so.
But he got well because tuberculosis, you can cure that, especially now, they tell me they can get it out quick.

I think what happened -- if I remember the story correctly, is that the band was playing in Texas, and there was somebody there giving free lung X-rays at the hotel where the band was, and so I think Duke had everybody go get one, because, you know, Duke was always so health concious, and it turned out that Cootie's X-Ray showed that he had TB, and so he left the band and rested for awhile, and then I think he played briefly with Mercer after Duke died; I'm not sure, but now he's not working at all.

I visited Al Sears and his wife when I was in New York last summer, and Cootie lives near them, and he said that Cootie and his wife went to the race track every day, and just enjoyed life, and relaxed -- and that he doesn't work because he doesn't want to, and he's doing very well.
Oh? I imagine he don't play that much.
The last time I heard Cootie play was the concert that Duke played here and there were so many people out here, way outside on Beverly Wilshire, or someplace; a concert that was given
there; there were a lot of people.
One of the Sacred concerts? The one in the Catholic Church? St. Paul's?
Yeah, yeah.
Paul Gonsalves played so beautifully that night, remember?

Yeah, I went over there with a friend of mine who took me over, and I went to his dressing room where he was laying down on the couch, and the doctor trying to fix him up because he had no money, you know? I said, 'Hi Duke' and he raised his arm, his left hand, and shook hands with him; I mean, he was sick.
That was when he did the television show at the Shubert Theatre. Yeah, that was the year before he did; in January of 1973 when Duke had the pneumonia. Yeah, and he was at the Century Plaza.

Well, finally, they started the show, and he came in in the front, and looked bad, and he shook hands. I happened to be in the front seat, because they let two front seats for me, but he didn't see me. But he went and shook hands with a couple of fellows in the front, but he said what he had to say and whatever he played, he played. But he really was a sick man.
He had 103 temperature when he got out of bed to go do that, because we were sitting with him over at the hotel -- Bob Udakoff and Stanley Dance.
And I saw him, too, when he was at the hospital, and in the hospital, I went over there when he was leaving -- another time, that I saw him, he was leaving one of those big hotels in Beverly Hills.
Yes, the Beverly Wilshire -- after he left St. Vincent's Hospital.
Yeah, and Rose fixed him some food and I took it over there.
And he was at the Beverly Wilshire until he got his strength back.
Yeah, he was paying $90 a day there.

And he had a good time over at the hospital when he started feeling better; he would call his friends up and tell them how to get in the back way, so that they wouldn't run in to the hospital officials, and he practically had a party up there every night.

Oh, he didn't care; as long as he had his comfort, he didn't care nothing about dollars. The dollars didn't mean nothing to him; he'd spend anything, only wanted his comfort. If he wanted a steak three inches high, give it to him and don't ask any questions. Anything -- a room or a suite, if it cost $50 a day, that's what I want. I want that.
Was he always like that? I know he was like that later.
Oh, he was.
Way back in the beginning?
He would always say he liked his comfort. He used to say there was no use trying to look out for the money you spend; you won't be living all your life, so you might as well enjoy it while you can.
Well, he always had the best he could get, and that's good.

Some fellow wrote me and they said they're trying to give an affair dedicated to you, and we would like to have some of your compositions; to write them down and write a letter with your compositions and this and that, and he started talking about the different people that were going to meet me, like this actor, a Puerto Rican fellow, that was raised in Puerto Rico -- what's his name, a dramatic actor --
I don't know ...
Jose Ferrer.
Jose Ferrer? Oh, he is Puerto Rican? I didn't know that.
Sure, he was born in Puerto Rico.
Oh?

And he was going to be one of the fellows to meet me and so forth, and for quite awhile, I thought it was gonna be a very good thing; I don't know if I was going to go to Puerto Rico -- because I don't like to
fly, and that takes quite a long time to get there, because we have four hours difference, you know?
Uh huh.

So the fellow later on, I found out -- oh no, I had my cousin in that picture, to find out about this man. And she went and reported and found out later that I think he had killed himself, after they started making plans to do this affair for me, I think he went broke or something happened with the business, and I think he killed himself.
How long ago was this that they were planning this?
Oh, it was about a year and a half ago or so; something like that.
Gee, well somebody else ought to do it then. Now.
Well, that was in Puerto Rico. I don't know, about that now.
When you went back to Puerto Rico before, after 44 years, what was different? How had things changed?

Well, outside the capital is a beautiful thing; all these big hotels with gambling and shows and this and the other -- and the towns near San Juan is all improved. Only San Juan, they wanted to keep it the old

San Juan, the old style, like the old Spanish people. The stores and the streets, you know? Very narrow streets, and I don't know what you call it -- the stone material the streets are made of, cement, you know?
Cobblestone?

Yeah, something like that. Oh, no, that is still the same way. The Plaza, I used to go there and I would skate, when I was in the band, and I thought the Plaza was so terrific, and when I went there again, I thought it was nothing. Oh, it changed so much -- it looks so different.

So they invited me one time for the television -- of course, they have two televisions where they speak English, just like you're doing now -- you know, asking you questions and this and the other, and one in English and one in Spanish, so they called me one time at the hotel for an interview, and as I said, they came and got me -- no, I went over, they say, 'You take a taxicab and I pay your fare, I meet you at such and such a hotel, outside of San Juan.'

I did that -- I came over, and I went to the studio and they had a little three piece band there, and this fellow interviewed me about me and my music and this and the other and Caravan and Perdido and so forth like that and they played, the three piece band, played Caravan - oh, it was a wonderful thing. So he brought me back to my hotel. So I don't know what else to say.
of San Juan. MS. WILLARD: You were telling me about the Association

When I went there in '69, the President of the Association -- what do they call it -- something about the San Juan something or other, I don't know what they call it, but anyhow, he gave me an autograph to me with all the different Puerto Rican dancers, and there was a fellow, a very good composer in there that I never met, I had never heard of him until I left, and he wrote all the music describing ... because we got a lot of vendors in Puerto Rico at that time, a fellow that sells bottles; a fellow who sells gas for cooking, or whatever, and a fellow that sells stuff for sewing and things like that.

And the food -- and whatever they sell, they have a lot of vendors. And carnivals, oh, we have parades just like New Orleans, and people put different kind of costumes on and they dance and do everything like that. So I lost what I was talking about.
You were telling me about the day they have once a year -- it starts early in the morning with the mass.
Yeah. Then we have the lunch, and then we have a dance.
Had breakfast after mass.
Yeah.
And you said the Association was
old San Juan.

The old San Juan, yes. And he autographed this program describing my music, how the peanut vendor used to go, you know? The peanut vendor or the fellow who sells the bottles for the parades and carnivals. It was wonderful.
Why don't you tell her about the day they were going to have for you?
I already told that.
Well, he did tell me -- you were in the other room.
Oh.

Oh, they always want me to -- they wrote me; they always write me a letter about this time of the year for me to come over. You notice what they always say at the bottom? 'We're expecting you'. But like I said before, I don't like airplanes.
Did you tell her that Sunchy and her husband came to the United States and came to see you?
Oh, that's my niece, one of the girls in the family.
That was the first time I had ever met them, they're lovely people. and she's just lovely.
Because her husband now is an agent for an insurance company, you know?
Uh huh.

And they travel a lot. Like in her last letter last week, she told me they are having their next convention in Miami, Florida, and they will come to New York to look at some clothes, and they may pass here, in Los Angeles, and naturally, when they do they will call.
Her husband has his office in his home.
Her name is what?
Her name is Sunchy. We call her that to be cute; like my mother doesn't call me Juan; she calls me Juanito. You know?
Duke used to call you Juanito, too.
Yeah.
S-u-n-c-h-y. Sunchy. Rodriguez.
Yeah, that's one of the daughters of my uncle, the musician.
Oh. And her last name now is Rodriguez.
He had four of them.
What is your niece's husband's name?
Oh, Sunchy's husband?
Uh huh.
He is an agent for an insurance company.
No, Juan, what is his name?
Oh, his name? Gonzales is his last name. Edyardo.
Edyardo Gonzales?
Yeah.
And a nice man; she got a nice husband. Takes her everywhere he goes.
Oh, they go everywhere; they've been to Spain, they've been everywhere.
He is Cuban.

He is Cuban, but now he don't want to, because he's trying to file -- in Puerto Rico, they want to be independent, you know? Some group wants Puerto Rico to be independent, which I don't like, because the first time I hear that Puerto Rico goes independent, I'm going to go downtown and tell them I am still an American citizen; I don't want no independence. Udkoff's?

Udkoff
And we stayed there until twelve or one o'clock

Yeah. The 600 Club.

Yeah.
Good.

Oh, sure, I had to. They wouldn't believe you -- I had to show my birth certificate; I used to tell them I was a Puerto Rican, and they said, 'What do you mean? Anybody can say they are Puerto Rican. You got to show me something to back it up.'

No, no. I think he is in Pennsylvania somewhere -- near Philadelphia.
Pennsylvania somewhere.

I know. Except money.

No. No.

Disappeared in Europe with ...

Forty.
Forty? $40,000. Yeah.

Oh, I don't want to mention that.

Can't do anything because it hasn't

Well, Al Kelley was not the nicest person in the world, but he did have a brilliant mind and was a great mathematician, and I don't think he had any doubt what he did; I think he knew -- he didn't have to write it down. I think he knew every penny he spent.
Yeah, he had a good mind.
He was a very, very brilliant man.
And he was very nice to me.

Oh yeah.

And what was so funny was that he would make a lot of mistakes because of his bad vision, except with money -- but he never made a mistake with money. People in the band used to say that he could feel the numbers on the bills, or smell the difference. You know how he would

Did the title come from the lyrics? Did you have anything to do with the title of that one?
No.

"Baker," "Bakeef," we talked a little bit before, and that was after Mills, so that would've been with Temple. Tempo. Then, "Moon Over Cuba" -- and that one says Tizol and Ellington. That one you wrote alone?
Uh huh.
Arranged by Duke. Do you remember anything special about that or how you happened to write it?
No, I don't know. No.
Okay. How about "Admiration?" Also called "Admiration Stomp."
That was one of the first tunes I wrote
outside of "Caravan" and "Perdido" -- "Admiration," I wrote that later on.

Yeah, because it was recorded in 1930, so that wasn't too long after you were with the band. March 20, 1930, on Brunswick, with Johnny, Barnie, Harry, Arthur Whetsol, Tricky Sam, Duke, Sonny Greer. Freddie Guy, Wellman Braud, and Sonny Greer.
Uh huh.
That one doesn't have Ellington's name on it. It just says Tizol and Mills.
Well, Duke got away that time.
How about "Jubilesta?"

"Jubilesta, Jubilesta." That was a nice tune that Cootie recorded. Cootie played the lead chorus on "Jubilesta" in the recording. Just like I said, Duke would just make the arrangements and we would record them.
And "Stevadore Serenade."
What?
"The Stevadore Serenade."
Oh, I don't know anything about that.
It says 1930 -- Ellington, Tizol, Gordon and Singer again.
Well, unless when I wrote it and they started to publish it, maybe the publisher gave it that name.
I think I have that record. Then
"Night Song" in 1939, and the credit there says Tizol and Mundy.
Jimmie Mundy, yeah.
Yeah, that's right.
I figured it was Jimmie Munday,
but ...
Charlie Barnett recorded that.
Oh? And apparently, Duke did too,
right?
I don't know if Duke arranged that tune or what.
Well, the only two names on it are Tizol and Mundy.
Yeah.
Probably Mundy arranged it.
Yeah, maybe so. I don't know.
And then you mentioned to me a little earlier today when I first got here, a tune called Keblah?
"Keblah," yes.
K-e-b-l-a-h.
That's right, "Keblah."
I don't find that one in the Ellington discographies or did Duke do that?
That was on the Crescendo publisher -- that was Mills-- or, oh, what was his name, the accountant for
Duke Ellington? Midler.
Midler.
Bill Midler.
I think he was President of Crescendo, or something like that -- the Crescendo Music Company, you know?
And was that recorded by Duke, or was it recorded?
Yes.
Harry James recorded it.
I see.
Duke must have recorded it, too, because you got a check, remember? And you couldn't have gotten a check if it hadn't been recorded.
Yeah, but that wouldn't make no difference -- anybody could have recorded it.
But didn't Harry James ...
I think that was a Harry James record.
I think he did, too. Yes.

Was there anything else you wrote for James, because I don't have a James discography. Did you do anything else besides these numbers? Did you write any new numbers that Harry James recorded that had not been done by Duke?
The Sphinx.
'The Sphinx?'
Do you remember that one?
I do remember.
You wrote // You Can't Have Your Cake and Eat It, Too, // while you were with Harry James, didn't you Juan?
Yeah. I recorded that with my own small group, and Willie Smith sang the lyrics.
Yes, I think you mentioned that before. Who published the tunes you wrote when you were with Harry?
This particular tune?
Uh huh.
// You Can't Have Your Cake and Eat It? //
I think that was Robbins.

Oh, I see. And then there was one I found on Louie Bellson's first record, which was done in the early fifties. It was called the Just Jazz All Stars, featuring Louie Bellson, but Louie was the leader.
What was the name?

The name of the album was called the Just Jazz All Stars featuring Louie Bellson, but it was done here in Los Angeles while the band was in town. And you're on the record; the people on the record are Willie Smith, Harry Carney, Wardell Gray, Juan Tizol, Clark Terry, Billy Strayhorn, John Graas-- the french horn player -- remember him -- and Wendell Marshall and Louie. And it was recorded

by Gene Norman for Capital Records -- a 10 inch LP, and Duke was in the booth, because I was there at the session and I remember. Billy Strayhorn was playing the piano, and a couple of the tunes are by Louie, but there was one by you called "Rainbow," and you played a solo on it. It's very pretty -- I played it last night. Do you remember that?
I do.
You do.

No, I don't remember myself. Oh, I did so many things like a fool, and I gave it to so many publishers; I gave it to Robbins Rollins, I gave it to Leefs, and I never hear about it -- like I told you before, these five tunes, which I would like to one of these days, if you tell me how to get to Irving Mills, I'm going to ask him about these brand new five tunes that I gave to him and never heard any more about. They made some copies, some piano parts, you know? And we recorded -- maybe it didn't come out good or something, with a small group, but I never heard no more about it, and they got lyrics to it, which I forgot the name of the fellow that wrote the lyrics for the five tunes -- 5 or 6 tunes.

Irving Mills sold Mills Music, but Irving Mills is still active, and he is still collecting all of his composer royalties. I'll give his address and phone number to you, because he's right here in Westwood, and you can ask him.
Sure, I do want to ask him about that.
But the first time I heard that Irving Mills got one of these publishers outside somewhere of New York, I don't know where it is.
I don't know. Well, he told me when I talked to him about a year ago that he did not have a publishing company now and that was why he wanted to buy Temple. He said he missed being a publisher.
Because his brother was the main person in the publishing company; the brother of Irving Mills. He was the big person, president or something.
What was Irving's brother's name? I don't know.
I don't, but he was a big shot there. I don't remember his name though.
Do you remember what tunes of yours that you gave to Leeds?
I get my papers, you know, from what I make, because they gave me so much money -- they loaned me one time an advance of four or five hundred dollars, and still they take it out every time.
How long ago was that?
Oh, that was a long time ago.
That's Robbins, wasn't it, Juan?
It was Robbins.
Oh, I thought you said Leeds.
No, no.

Now we've mentioned the tunes that you had with various publishing companies, but you said you gave some to Leeds, and I just wondered if there were tunes that we hadn't mentioned yet, and I wanted to get them if we haven't gotten it yet.
I can't remember. I know I went once to the office myself and I talked to Lee and I showed him the every thing, and he said he liked it. Well, later on, I don't know what happened.
You don't remember?
No, no.

I was trying to find out if I could what the first record was that you made after you joined the band, the first time you recorded with Duke, and according to the discography here, your first record was made on September 13th, 1929, your first recording date -- and did 'Jallywog', 'Jazz Convulsions' and 'Slow Motion' -- those were the names of the tunes that you recorded on your first record date. Do you remember anything about your first record date?
No.
That's a long time ago, I know.

Well, Juan's first record date was with Duke Ellington before he joined the band. He sent for signed Juan to make a record date with him. Do you remember, Juan? He sent for you to make a record date when you were at Paco's house. And he told you that he'd be sending for you,
that he liked your work and he would be sending for you. And you made a record date with him.
I've got a question about that. May I see that book? I think it was Gunther Schuler's book where he says he suspects that that is Juan on the record, if I can find it here.
Rose, you were just saying what you remembered about Juan's first record date with Duke; that Juan was working with Cliff Jackson, you said?

He was working with Cliff Jackson, in Newark, and his first date with Duke wasn't a record date; it was a broadcast, and Ted Heusen was the announcer, and somebody in the band, I don't know who it was, was sick or out or quit, I don't know which it was -- and he asked for Juan, if he would come up and play that broadcast for him.

And he told Juan he'd be sending for him, and he sent for him to make a record date with him, and he told Juan that he liked him and he would be sending for him. Afterwards, he left New York and went back home to Washington D.C., and Arthur Whetsel called up and said that Duke would like to have Juan in the band.
And that's when Juan joined the band.
Thank you. So you played with Duke for a radio broadcast before you joined the band, then?
Oh, yes --just for one date only.
Was that at the Cotton Club?
At the Cotton Club, yeah.
I see.
They used to broadcast every evening at six o'clock.
Uh huh.
And Ted Heuser was the announcer.
At six o'clock, so you came into the radio broadcast and then you left again, because the show didn't start that early, right?

But I left, you know? Because I didn't know if Duke was going to use me any more, but he told me, "I'm going to send for you one of these days," and that's when he called me in Washington, to come for the Zigfeld Follies, you know?
Do you remember how much time passed before ...

No, I don't know too much about how long it was, because like I said, we had a little business and we were tending to the delicatessen store, you know, and I used to play a little gig here and there, in Washington, and all of a sudden, that telephone call came from Duke for me to come to New York because he was getting ready to start the Zigfeld Follies. So I said, "Well, sure --" and I left her over there to take care of the deli and sell it while I was in New York.
So I used to do two shows -- the Cotton Club and
The Zigfeld Follies.
What was the name of your delicatessan? The Tizol Delicatessen?
Just Tizol's Delicatessan. That's all.
I see.
And then after I sold it, I went to New York to join him, which wasn't very long. It didn't take me long to sell it, because we had a pretty good little business there.
Whereabouts was it located?
On Rhode Island Avenue. Fifth and Rhode Island Avenue in Northwest Washington, D.C.
I used to eat all the ice cream instead of selling it. We used to take home about a quart or something like that home every evening.
So you're an ice cream fan, too, like Duke is.
So you and Duke used to eat ice cream together?
Oh, I guess so. Duke used to send me some of that rich ice cream they sold around here -- what was that name of the ice cream ...
(Willrights?)
Will Wrights? That was his favorite kind, I know.
Yeah. He used to send me some of that.
Oh yes, Duke always wanted ice cream.

His only complaint, I think, about St. Vincent's Hospital, when he was in there with pneumonia, was that Bobbie Udokoff brought him all different flavors of Willright's ice cream, and Duke said that somebody was stealing the chocolate, because they kept it in the hospital freezer, and Duke said every time he sent the nurse to get him some chocolate, the chocolate was all gone.
(Interruption)
He made the arrangements and he got credit for it.
Yeah, let him take the credit, but I want them to know who wrote the music, which is right -- am I right, Juan?
Well, maybe he changed something in there, in the middle or somewhere, Rose. Because there were two different middle parts on Caravan, you know?
There were?
I think so.
You think so -- but you don't know.
Yeah, I think they wrote two different ones, and I think that's what Duke did, so you got to give him credit for that, Rose.
Well, you think so, but you don't know.
Do you remember how the part that Duke may have written went?
No.
The one they published.
Well, how did the one you wrote go? The middle part. Can you hum it?
Da, da, da ... oh, I can't sing. It was different than the one Duke wrote.
So he changed the middle, then.
He changed that thing. That's what I said -- he deserved credit for that, Rose.
You just mentioned another tune that we didn't before. Was that 'Zanzibar'?
'Zanzibar,' yeah.
And you wrote that and it was recorded by whom?
I recorded that myself with my small group. Here in California, when Willie Smith was doing 'You Can't Have Your Cake' -- it was around the same time.
And who else was in that small group besides Willie?
(Dick Cathcart, Babe Russin, Arnold Ross, Irving Ashby, E. Mihelich, Nick Fatool -- ed.)
The trumpet player was a white fellow; I don't know his name -- I forgot.
(Dick Cathcart -- ed.)
The guys with Harry James' band.

That drummer -- I know he used to do a lot of recordings around here, but I don't know -- I don't hear about him any more. I just can't remember ... no, I can't remember who else was there besides Willie, the drummer, I mean, Willie and the trumpet player. I just don't know.
(Nick Fatool -- ed.)

The question I wanted to ask you from the book by Gunther Schuler called Early Jazz -- Its Foots and Musical Development, he discusses the recording of "Tiger Rag" by Duke, which was in January of 1929 -- it was January 8, 1929, which was about 8 or 9 months before you joined Duke's band.

So he says here that Ellington's band presented a staggering array of nongimmicky, highly individual solos. Even Bigard's chromatic run, under other circumstances of a fairly tawdry ideas, had in this context a drive that turns it into the high point of the record. ""

And then there is a footnote saying, "Hearing this record, one also tends to suspect that Juan Tizol was already a member, or perhaps just a guest that day in the trombone section. I find it fairly hard otherwise, to explain the low B flat trombone trill just before Freddie Jenkins' famous chorus. ""

Now according to the discography, the only trombone player on there was Tricky Turkey Sam, and so apparently, Dr. Gunther Schuler doesn't feel that Tricky Turkey Sam could have played that. Do you remember ever doing a recording with Duke before you joined the band, earlier that same year?
On Tiger Rag? ""
On Tiger Rag. ""
I don't know.
You know, he sent for you to do a
recording, Juan -- maybe that was the one.
I don't know about Tiger Rag -- I don't know.
You don't remember the names of tunes.
You don't remember what you played, though, do you? It could have been Tiger Rag.
It is was all so far away long ago, you know?
Yeah, but I remember he sent for you to do a recording before you joined the band.
I think I have that record at home. I should have brought it, but I was just carrying so much stuff today. If you heard it, do you think you tell if you were on it?
I don't know -- I'd have to hear it, you know?
That's what she said -- if you heard it, could you tell.

I don't know, because I know darn well even if I heard it, I don't know if I was not featured or anything, because I know well that on Tiger Rag, at that particular time, I couldn't even take no solos on Tiger Rag.
He doesn't say anything about solos, it just says that ...
I was just played-ing the part that was written, that's all -- just played the music.
The low B flat trombone trill just before Freddie Jenkins' famous chorus. That's the part he
My trombone wasn't a B flat -- it was a C trombone. I never played a B flat trombone.
(Interruption)
You were talking about a magazine in Washington?
What was it called -- what was the name of that thing?
What?
They used to come years ago when I first joined tha band. They would write about anything that happened, you know?
A little magazine in Washington.
Hanging around the Puerto Rican boys and so forth.
No, I don't remember.
Well, what was it they said about you?

Well, they were talking one time about some chicks that were following me backstage or at the entrance or something, you know, waiting for Juan Tizol, the Puerto Rican something -- I don't know what they called me, I forgot.
Rose just found an article in the scrapbook that called you a pale Cuban.
Yeah?

In the New Yorker profile on Duke Ellington, Richard Boyer quotes you as saying when you were he was traveling with the band -- 'When we don't get sleep' -- We don't sleep, said Tizol, who was Puerto Rican and the only white man in the band, 'it seems like our lips get even stronger; you get a lot of sleep, and damn it if they don't crumble.' " Is that an experience that you remember?
I didn't get that.
Oh. They quote you as saying that when you don't get any sleep, it made your lips stronger, it seemed like and when you got a lot of sleep, you didn't have as strong a lip. Do you remember that?
No.

And there was another passage in the same article where it said that you were in a gloomy mood and you asked Duke what he saw in your playing anyway, and he said, 'You don't call yourself a hot man; take all your solos straight and sweet'. " And, Duke was supposed to have said to you, 'There are times when a writer wants to hear something exactly as it's written, you want to hear it clean -- not with smears and slides on it; besides, your style is good contrast to Johnny Hodges' " --and it quotes you as saying, 'I play with a legit tone. Duke, what is there about my trombone tone?'"

And Duke said, to you, 'You get an entirely different quality. It's real accurate; so many look upon the valve trombone as an auxillary instrument, and it's your main instrument -- and that's a hell of an obligation; you got to live up to those valves, and you do, Juan, you do. You know how many slide trombonists use a slide so they can fake? And when you object they say, 'What do you think it's got on it, valves?' If there was any room in legit, you say, 'I'd still go back to legit. I like legit because I can feature myself better in legit than in a jazz band. I don't feel the pop tunes, but I feel La Boheme.' I like that pure romantic flavor, I can feel that better.'
Then Duke said to the room at large, 'Juan has got inhibitions; he won't ad lib. Once on the Twelfth Street Rag he did some ad libbing, only time he ever did.'
Is that true?
I guess so-- if he says so.
Do you remember ad libbing on Twelfth Street Rag?

I know Barney was telling me about that one time we were recording one of those things -- I don't know if it was that or 'Dinah,' and I was supposed to take a break on it and I did something terrific, and I stopped and they recorded it. And Duke, said, 'Why did you stop? That was terrific!' (laugh)
Do you remember why you stopped?
I thought I was doing something wrong on it.
Oh! Too bad ...
(Interruption)
Do you want me to read the New Yorker?
you?
Yeah. Rose was looking through the scrapbook here and she found a piece here.

New York, July 20th -- Duke Ellington's return to the United States has been set back to August 5th to be exact, because a new engagement was contracted as a result of his popularity. He concluded three weeks at the Palladium in London last week and then went to Holland for four concerts for the weeks of July 21st and 28th at the Rex in Paris. He will return on The Majestic.
Thank you.
I got something else here.
What do you have?
The highest salary every paid by the British Broadcasting Company to an orchestra was drawn by Duke Ellington and his band for a 45-minute broadcast from London.
That would have been, when? 1939?
I haven't got the date.
Oh.
// Juan Tizol, trombone. Musically, the most thoroughly educated man in the band. Arrived from Puerto Rico to play symphony. Still plays valve trombone. Goes
into raptures over Spanish music. Dances a [plenty] solo rhumba.
And that was from an article from about the same period. Juan, could you tell me about your dancing?

Oh, with Harry James and his wife, you know, we were going to Las Vegas -- only a small group, just one trombone, a trumpet and three saxophones, and the drummer, who was -- oh, who was it? The best drummer -- supposed to be the best white drummer in the business.
Buddy somebody ...
Buddy Rich.
Buddy Rich, yeah. But we went there with his wife.
Betty Grable?

Betty Grable, and they used to play -- we used to feature it in Caravan, which was like I said before, was arranged by Neal Hefti. And I had a little thing at the end, and at the end, the drummer kept on going, and nobody told me to do it -- I just did it for the first time, you know? So he told me to go out on the front of the stage, and I started dancing, doing a few steps and I did that movement that some people laugh at. But they kept it in.
So you kept doing it in the show?
I kept doing it in the show, and at the end, by the time I did the cadenza, I said, 'Harry, I don't believe I can make it'. You know, that's on the stage.
"I can't make it". And Harry said, "Oh, go ahead, Juan -- go ahead. You can do it; go on." So I had to go ahead and do it. I had a pretty good audience to clap for me, you know, give me the business.
Well, from what Rose was saying from that article, it sounded like you were also dancing when you were with Duke. He said you did a good solo rumba.
Solo?
A dance -- when you were with Duke.

When we were in theatres, I used to play the tambourine; I used to shake myself, you know? I was not dancing particularly on stage out there; when the band was playing, I was just playing the tambourine, and I used to shake myself, you know?
Spanish style. Listen.
That article I read to you was from a French magazine, you know.
Oh. So that was probably during that same trip then.
In Europe, yes.
Do you know the name of the magazine? Is it on there?
It says Dance Band Reviews by George Simon. Simer.
Uh huh. George Simon.
And it says Cotton Club -- and then they have a picture of the band. See?
Yeah. Oh, that's from Metronome, April, 1937. Yes, I see.
Thank you.
But I think this man is a French guy that wrote this.

We were doing one nighters and we were going to play Flint, Michigan, you know? So he followed us in his Lincoln. Joe Louis. When we got through the dance, Joe Louis asked me and Duke and Sonny Greer -- we're going to a little cabaret, you know? And he got mad because he was charging, he was charging because Joe Louis was going to be there and he didn't like that. He said you are going to try to make money out of me, and so forth -- so he just didn't go in.

So we started back to Detroit, and he was trying to follow one of those -- I know the car, it was a real fast car, and he was doing 110 miles an hour. Oh my Lord, and that Sonny Greer was full of whiskey and would say, "Take them Champ! Take them!"
And a policeman stopped him and when he found out it was Joe Louis, but he still told us not to go that fast in there because you'll never live to be a champion, you know?
Uh huh. He didn't give him a ticket?
And every time I used to see after that -- No, no ticket -- Joe Louis, I used to tell him, "How about that 110 miles?" He used to laugh and say that when he
got to his hotel he had little things in his drawer, you know? I was scared to death.
That's pretty fast.
This is what the English critics wrote about Duke Ellington. Maybe you can get something from this.

Yeah, that's very interesting. In the Peter Gammond's book, he says about Washington, D.C. and the Howard Theatre, he said there was a flashy and competent character playing drums in the Howard Theatre, in a very professional band that also included Juan Tizol, the drummer with Sonny Greer. The Ellingtonian struck up an acquaintance with him, and soon Greer left the theatre orchestra to join up with them as well.
Now didn't you say that Sonny and you did not work in the same band, right, at the Howard?
Well, he was there; yeah, he was there in the pit, but not with our band -- that was before when the Puerto Rican people came in there.
But you and Sonny did not work in the same band at the Howard at the same time, though, did you? Is that what you're saying?
No, I don't think so.
So this is a little bit confused then. Okay. In Washington, did you know Elmer Snowden?
Elmer Snowden?
Uh huh.
Sure.
Did you ever play with him?

No, I didn't get a chance to play with him, no. I played with Doc Perry, the fellow that taught a lot of things to Duke Ellington -- the piano player -- he used to have a small band there, too. And like the White Brothers. I used to play with them -- I played at the Republic Theatre for legit pictures and so forth, like the // Four Horsemen // and so forth.
Oh? Uh huh.
We had a band there for that particular picture, you know? So I was playing the cello parts.
Oh, the cello parts?
Yeah.
That's interesting.
Wooding -- I don't know if you remember, what's his first name? Russell Wooding. A nice musician. He was there and he was the piano player at that particular time.
That was at the theatre.
At the theatre, yes.
What can you tell me about Elmer Snowden?
Who?
Elmer Snowden. What can you tell me about him?
Well, there's not much I can say about
him, because he was playing in different bands, I mean, his own band, doing gigs, and I never got a chance to play with him, so I don't know much about him.
Wellman Braud.
We talked about Wilma Brough. When you first came in the band, there were a lot of bass players that you worked with in Duke's band that we haven't mentioned. How about Hayes Alviss Albiss?

Well, he was a showman on the bass. You know, hitting the things and all, and stuff like that. He was a good bass player, but he let the people see the way he was playing and so forth -- you know, hitting the thing and what not.
Uh huh. How about Billy Taylor?
Oh, he was a good bass player, only he was just straight. He was a good man, though. He could eat, too!
A big appetite?
Ooo!
Bigger than Duke's?
Sure. He could eat plenty.
His wife said he could eat a pound of beans, and that's a lot of beans.
pound
A pound of beans?
That's an awful lot of beans.
It sure is. How about Jimmy Blanton?
Blanton? Oh, he was a great musician.

Jimmy Blanton -- I went to see him, we was in St. Louis, and I went to see Jimmy Blanton once, because he was a fellow who used to take his bass and play with anybody, you know? In this particular cabaret, I went there and listened to him, and he was playing Sophisticated Lady with a bow, you know? And he did so many good things in there, I go out of the club there and ran over to the hotel where we and Duke were staying, too, and I said, "Duke, you got to get up and come with me and let's go and see this bass player, to go and hear him."
And he did -- he came over there, and he said, "Man, he's terrific; I'm going to get that man." And he got him; he took him with him, then.
And I guess he was a pretty nice person, guy, huh?
He was a very good friend, they both used to stick together, him and Ben Webster.
Yeah, that's what I heard, yeah.
Ben Webster and him,, oh, they used to go together and in the dressing room in theatres, in their own dressing rooms, they used to jam on different tunes.
And how about after work? Did they go out jamming after work, too?
Well, any place Ben asked him to go, he would go, you know? He was such a wonderful, nice kid.
Yeah, everybody I know that knew him, that I've talked to, said marvelous things about Jimmy Blanton.
Yes, indeed.
And hwo about Oscar Pettiford?
You know, I don't know much about Pettiford. I know he did Perdido on the cello. I believe I have a record there.
Yeah, I think I have that, too. It's beautiful. How about Wendell Marshall?

He was another nice bass player, too. I don't know what kind of sickness he had, but the doctor used to tell him to eat raw potatoes. He would cut pieces of raw potatoes and eat it when he'd be at restuarants. I don't know what his trouble was.
I don't know, either. He was Jimmy Blanton's cousin, right?
Oh yeah.
And he played Jimmy Blanton's bass? Didn't he have the same instrument as Jimmy had?
How's that?
As I remember, he had Jimmy's bass, and he was playing Jimmy's bass in the band.
Well, I don't know. Maybe so.
I think so. That's what I heard. And you were saying -- you mentioned to me the other day the trombone player who came in after Tricky Sam, or did the same parts, and you
couldn't think of his name. But was that Tyree Glenn you were talking about?
No, that was White, I think. He came in there and played for awhile. I think now, I don't know.
How about Britt Woodman?
Bill Williams?
No, Britt Woodman.

Oh, he was a good trombone player. I played with him with Nelson Riddle, and then Nat Cole and did a few recordings and with Duke Ellington, he was the first trombone player, and he was a good man. I liked him -- he did a lot of work around here.
Juan, this was taken in New York. Because it has on the back of it, Please credit Bill Marks, 79 Riverside Drive, New York 29, New York.
That's the picture of you and Willie Smith on your way to Boston, right?
Right. Do you want to see a picture of Juan when he received his First Communion?
Oh, that's August 6th, 1906 when you received your First Communion.
He was 6 years old.
Six years old, yes.
Ah, you were a very cute little boy! How about Wardell Grey? He was on that album of Louie Bellson's
that you were on. Did you work with him any other time other than that one album?
Who?
Wardell Grey, the tenor saxophone player from Los Angeles. He was on that album that Louie did in the early fifties where you took a solo on 'Rainbow.'
I don't know him.
You didn't know Wardell?
No.
How about Don Byas?
John Byas?
DON Byas. Tenor saxophone player from Oklahoma, but he moved to L.A.
Oh, him, I never did play with him.
No.
How about Django Reinhardt?
With him? No.
